anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: The approved L1 mine exposes four diamonds in a 5x5x3 voxel pile with one lava hazard and one fragile support. A screenshot-only solver must choose viewpoints, read depth-sorted exposed faces, remove blockers, preserve support, and click precise ray-hit locations; the grader replays orientation, ray hits, durability, materials, and collapse. Lampwrights shares 3D/isometric spatial reading and target extraction, but its L4 task has a static map and no raycast, hazard, or continuous motor-control burden. It instead requires inferring a legal reusable command program over five marked tiles and a 27-command generated route witness. This is a different burden, but it is materially above the mine's simple four-target L1 configuration in discrete planning.

evidence.explanation: The approved baseline is L1/simplified with four targets, one lava block, one support, and limited durability.
The generator constructs per-target seal/blocker/extraction steps, viewpoint-dependent ray points, and a hazard edge case.
The visible UI renders the voxel pile, durability, material legend, camera controls, and canvas ray-click interaction; full mode adds canvas dragging.
The grader independently replays rotations, resets, click-ray occlusion, material outcomes, durability, inventory, and support collapse.

anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: The approved L3 gyro board has three ordered lamps, three walls, three wells, momentum, 50 ms physics ticks, and a full analog-drag surface. Its screenshot-only solution must continuously steer a moving ball, interpret position and velocity, avoid resets, and settle in the cup; the grader checks every physics tick and enforces minimum ticks and control changes. Lampwrights L4 has substantially less temporal and motor-control demand because the route is evaluated from a static program and the execution animation can be waited out. Its extra burden is discrete spatial planning and procedure reuse: five target tiles, four generated jump transitions, changing headings, and a seven-call main routine. The L4 placement is plausible as a composite difficulty judgment, but the two tasks are not strictly ordered on every capability.

evidence.explanation: The approved baseline is L3/full with three lamps, three walls and hazards, 50 ms ticks, and a 500 ms multi-frame observation setting.
The generator creates ordered switches, walls, wells, physics constants, and solver waypoints for the L3 contract.
The visible implementation advances velocity and position on physics ticks, handles wall/hazard contacts, and exposes analog or compass input.
The grader replays deterministic physics and checks input source, tick state, ordered lamps, minimum ticks, controls, and final cup completion.

anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: The approved L5 candy task requires four adjacent swaps on a changing 5x5 board, deterministic multi-wave cascades, an exact score, a short refill preview, and untouched black licorice. Each accepted swap changes the board, refill cursor, score, and future options, so the next decision depends on the previous action. Lampwrights L4 has five targets and a longer discrete route, but the world does not change while the agent is choosing successive commands; it is a static route/program reconstruction with visible target and height geometry. It is therefore below this L5 anchor in state-dependent search and exact-score constraints, while remaining harder than a simple static placement task.

evidence.explanation: The approved baseline is L5/simplified with a four-move changing-board route, at least seven total cascade waves, and only five preview candies.
The generator enumerates routes over changing boards, resolves deterministic refills and waves, and chooses an exact-score four-swap instance.
The visible UI performs adjacent swaps, cascades, gravity/refill, score updates, and terminal overpay/short-change handling through either clicks or drag.
The grader replays each swap and cascade, checks exact board/score/refill state, enforces the move budget and wave threshold, and rejects licorice contact.

visible_baseline_solution: A normal screenshot-only solver must read the isometric rooftop rather than private state: identify the robot start pose and heading, distinguish every marked lamp tile from unmarked stepped blocks and decoys, and infer a route through the visible height map. It must choose F for a same-height neighbor, J for exactly one height change, L/R for heading changes, and G only while standing on a marked tile. At the L4 baseline it must compose the main procedure and the amber and blue routines, place the instruction glyphs into the visible slots using full drag-and-drop, run the program, inspect the blocked or completed feedback, revise if needed, wait for the step playback to finish, and certify. Success is all distinct visible targets lit by a program that independently replays within the three panel slot limits; target labels are visible, but the grader checks the target set rather than requiring a particular target order. The run has slot-placement precision and discrete planning demands, not a continuously timed steering requirement.

baseline_judgment.rationale: Keep L4/full. The L4 profile changes the actual decision problem: five marked targets are embedded in a height-sensitive isometric route, the generated witness has 27 primitive commands, and the seven-call main procedure reuses two six-command routines from changing headings. The browser checks terrain height for F versus J and the independent grader replays the submitted program and requires every target to be lit. This is more discrete planning than the approved L1 mine and comparable in planning burden to or above the approved L3 gyro, although it lacks the gyro's continuous momentum and temporal control. It remains below the approved L5 candy anchor's changing-board exact-score search. The source supports the current label, but it does not establish empirical completion-rate ordering.

evidence.explanation: The baseline profile has eight main slots, six routine slots, ten decorations, two decoration height values, and a seven-call reusable program.
The generator expands procedure calls, updates heading and height, makes F/J terrain transitions, and records marked target positions and the route witness.
The browser evaluates the submitted routine against the visible terrain, rejects illegal height moves or off-roof moves, and requires the full target set to be lit.
The independent replay enforces movement, one-height jumps, legal light commands, nesting/execution bounds, and equality between lit targets and the generated target set.
Certification is bound to the challenge and condition, then independently replays the program and checks a completed execution transcript.

uncertainties: The generated route length is a construction witness, not a proof that every seed or target set requires that many decisions; alternate valid programs are allowed.
No human or computer-use-agent completion-rate calibration was available in this source-only audit.

findings.claim: The grader does not require editor_events to be nonempty or to describe the submitted final program.
findings.causal_explanation: grade() accepts any list of at most 400 editor events and checks only the input_source of events that are present. It then independently replays the separately submitted program. A direct payload can therefore provide a valid program with an empty editor_events list, and execution_events are likewise checked only for a run_complete marker and a matching step count, not for their command/state fields. Ordinary browser UI transcripts do carry the correct source and wrong populated sources are rejected, but the grading contract does not prove that the selected input surface produced the program.

evidence.explanation: The editor list may be empty; program replay is independent; execution events are reduced to marker/count checks.
The browser does record edit events, so the gap is in the grader's required binding rather than the normal UI's event production.

findings.recommended_action: Require a nonempty canonical edit transcript and replay each place, erase, and reorder against an initially empty editor, or otherwise cryptographically/canonically bind the final program to the recorded input events. Validate execution event contents rather than only their count.

findings.claim: height_variation does not control route elevation changes; it only changes random decoration-block heights.
findings.causal_explanation: _run_program creates all route heights from J and the alternating jump rule before _build_world receives height_variation. The only use of height_variation is the random height assigned while appending decoration blocks. Those blocks can add visible 3D clutter, but the parameter does not make the required route contain more height transitions. The profile summaries should not be read as evidence that this parameter changes the robot's route physics.

evidence.explanation: Route height is determined by F/J and jump_number inside _run_program.
height_variation is passed to _build_world and used only for decoration candidate heights.
The parameter changes across profiles, while the profile program itself supplies the route J commands.

findings.recommended_action: Document height_variation as decoration-only and calibrate whether the added clutter is materially harder, or add a separate route-elevation parameter if route height complexity is intended.

affected_configurations: all five difficulty levels across seeds
findings.claim: For a fixed level, the substantive target route is seed-invariant; seeds randomize decoration placement/heights rather than the program, target geometry, headings, or route.
findings.causal_explanation: Each level's program is a literal constant in PROFILES. The seed initializes the RNG used by _build_world, but _run_program derives terrain, targets, and route solely from that fixed program; randomness is applied when choosing decoration candidates and their heights. This gives visible decoy variation but limited held-out variation in the core planning problem, despite the large generator variant_count metadata.

evidence.explanation: The five level programs are fixed constants and the seed only initializes a random source.
The route and target construction consumes the program before decoration randomness is introduced.
The random candidate blocks are appended after the fixed route and targets.

findings.recommended_action: Treat seed diversity as decoration/visual-clutter diversity in calibration, not as independent route instances; if broader procedural difficulty is required, vary the route program or target topology.

findings.claim: L1 does not require reusable routine use even though its summary presents a reusable routine.
findings.causal_explanation: The L1 direct body G-F-J-G fits within the four main slots. The browser filters empty slots and evaluates any legal program, while the grader checks panel limits and replay but never requires A or B to be called. Thus routine reuse is optional at L1; it becomes a real capacity constraint only in higher profiles.

evidence.explanation: L1's A body is four commands and the main panel has four slots.
Empty slots are filtered and a direct main-panel program is evaluated normally.
The grader enforces panel limits and replay but has no routine-use requirement.

findings.recommended_action: Keep this as an intentional L1 simplification or change the L1 summary; only reduce main capacity if routine reuse is meant to be mandatory.

concise_summary: Keep Lampwrights Program at L4/full. The source shows a real progression from a short two-target route to a six-target reusable program with dependent heading and height state, and the L4 baseline sits above the L1/L3 anchors in discrete planning while below the changing-board L5 anchor. Record the transcript-binding, decoration-height, seed-variation, and optional-L1-reuse caveats.
limitations: This is source-only evidence; no browser, headless grader, exported verifier, multi-seed runtime, human, or computer-use-agent check was run.
No historical pre-controls implementation was available, so historical preservation is unverified.
The absolute L1-L5 assignments remain provisional without completion-rate and action/time calibration.
The route witnesses and private solver are implementation evidence, not proof of the shortest or only screenshot-only solution.
